title: Exomiser prioritization contributed to rare-disease diagnoses in the 100,000 Genomes Project pilot
summary: In an English National Health Service pilot, Exomiser ranked candidate variants for 2,183 families; 25% of probands got a genetic diagnosis, and a quarter of diagnoses were immediately actionable.
headline: Exomiser ranks gene variants and helps diagnose rare disease in England
metric: Genetic diagnoses were found in 25% of probands, rising to 35% for monogenic disorders
brief: From May 2016 through April 2019, a national rare-disease pilot of the 100,000 Genomes Project returned results to the Genomic Medicine Centers of the English National Health Service. Across 2,183 families, genetic diagnoses were found in 25% of probands, and clinicians reported that a quarter of the diagnoses could be acted on at once. Exomiser ranked candidate variants against each patient's phenotype. Of the 490 diagnoses based on single-nucleotide variants or indels, 88% were among Exomiser's top five candidates, and 92% were made with the applied gene panels or those candidates.[1] The pilot's authors report that one diagnosis enabled a curative bone marrow transplantation for a 10-year-old girl and that another let the younger brother of a baby who had died undiagnosed start weekly injections. They do not say whether Exomiser or the applied panels flagged either variant, so neither outcome can be credited to the software. In a later reanalysis across the full project, Exomiser ranked candidate variants again, and after manual interpretation of the ranked candidates, diagnoses were found for 463 of 24,015 patients whose cases the earlier analysis had left unsolved. In a separate deployment in Hong Kong, Exomiser ranked 67% of 132 diagnoses first.[2]

comparator_before: A total of 322 (66%) of the 490 diagnoses that were based on SNVs or indels from the genomes were made with the virtual panel–based pipeline
comparator_after: diagnoses were detected in 77% of the top-ranked candidate variants, in 86% of the top three candidates, and in 88% of the top five candidates

summary: An Embrace wristband detected a seizure that left Morgan McGrath, 26, of Fulton, Missouri, not breathing and alerted her mother, who called paramedics; IEEE Spectrum reports that she survived.
headline: *Embrace* wristband alerts a mother, and she calls paramedics
brief: In November 2016 Morgan McGrath, a 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri, had an epileptic seizure that left her unresponsive and not breathing.[1] Her Embrace wristband detected the seizure and alerted her mother, who called paramedics. McGrath survived, and her rescue rests on a single IEEE Spectrum report. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared the device on 26 January 2018, after the event.[2] Later evidence comes from hospital epilepsy monitoring units. In an independent study published on 7 January 2026, researchers in Montreal found that the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures that occurred while it was worn and working, with 29 false alarms in 373 days of monitoring. It detected none of 510 focal seizures without convulsions, a type that the device is not cleared to detect.[3]

metric: time on the ground fell by 29.6 minutes (95% CI 20.3 to 38.9)
brief: Between May and August 2018, staff in six California memory care facilities received real-time alerts from SafelyYou Guardian's AI video fall detection. In that period, residents with dementia spent on average 29.6 fewer minutes on the ground after a fall than in a baseline period without alerts, in November and December 2017. The share of fallers who lay on the ground for more than an hour fell from 31% (8 of 26) to none. In 97.6% of the falls, the resident could not stand up alone. The study compares periods in the same facilities without a concurrent control group, and every author had ties to SafelyYou.[1] In 2023, authors at Imperial College London, who declare no conflicts of interest, included the study in a synthesis of research on video recording for direct patient care. They listed the same reductions and read them as showing that the system improves care after falls.[2] In a year-long pilot in two South Australian aged care facilities, false alerts from AI video monitoring reportedly overwhelmed staff and contributed to a real event being missed.

brief: This case rests on one speaker. In a WIRED report of 19 June 2019, Thorn's chief executive, Julie Cordua, said that a California officer had run a missing child's photo through Spotlight. headline: Nigeria uses machine-learning poverty maps to target COVID-19 cash aid
metric: 49,000 beneficiary households as of 15 October 2021
brief: Nigeria had no urban social registry, so its National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office built the Rapid Response Register for a government-funded COVID-19 cash transfer. Using ward-level poverty maps made by applying machine-learning algorithms to satellite imagery, the government selected 1,163 of the poorest urban wards, with a population of over 20 million.[1] Residents of those wards then registered by mobile phone and were verified in person. The developers of the maps report that, in targeting the poor, the machine-learning approach raises ward-level precision to 0.92, against 0.79 for a survey-based benchmark.[2] No source shows how many people the maps helped. A World Bank status report of 29 January 2025 records 49,000 beneficiary households in the cash transfer as of 15 October 2021 and does not say how many had been paid. It also counts over 5 million households supported by the direct benefit transfer program, with no breakdown of the share that the register targeted.[3] Human Rights Watch researchers argued in July 2021 that the targeting methods had in all likelihood excluded, or would exclude, large numbers of people in need.[4]

title: Baricitinib, identified with BenevolentAI's knowledge graph, lowered COVID-19 deaths in the RECOVERY trial
summary: BenevolentAI researchers used the Benevolent Platform's knowledge graph to identify baricitinib for COVID-19, and in the RECOVERY trial mortality was 12% with the drug and 14% with usual care alone.
headline: Drug found with a knowledge graph lowered COVID-19 deaths in a trial
metric: mortality was 12% with the drug and 14% with usual care alone
brief: On 4 February 2020 BenevolentAI researchers reported in The Lancet that their knowledge graph had helped them identify baricitinib, an arthritis drug, as a possible treatment for COVID-19. In the ACTT-2 trial, 1,033 hospitalized adults received remdesivir with either baricitinib or a placebo, and median recovery took 7 days with baricitinib and 8 days with the placebo. In the COV-BARRIER trial, 8% of patients receiving baricitinib had died by day 28, compared with 13% receiving a placebo. Mortality was a secondary outcome in that trial, which did not meet its primary outcome of reduced disease progression.[1] In the later RECOVERY trial, 8,156 patients were randomly assigned to usual care with or without baricitinib, and mortality, its primary outcome, was 12% with baricitinib and 14% with usual care alone.[2] On 14 January 2022 the World Health Organization strongly recommended baricitinib with corticosteroids for patients with severe or critical COVID-19. On 10 May 2022 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved baricitinib for hospitalized adults with COVID-19 who need supplemental oxygen or other respiratory support. In Europe, Eli Lilly withdrew its application on 7 December 2022 after the European Medicines Agency reached the provisional opinion that three trials did not conclusively show meaningful benefit.[3] None of the trials compared discovery with AI against discovery without it, and the knowledge graph's part in the choice rests on a letter and a methods paper by BenevolentAI researchers.[4]

brief: The Bieszczady Mountain Rescue Service called this the first find in Poland of a missing person using a drone and SARUAV.[1] A 65-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease had left home in Cergowa a day after a stroke, and police with tracking dogs did not find him after a storm. summary: A smartwatch of unstated brand alerted a 58-year-old man to an irregular heart rate above 180 beats per minute; the care that followed found a lung adenocarcinoma, which surgeons removed.
headline: Smartwatch flags a racing heart, and follow-up care finds lung cancer
metric: The 35 mm tumor was staged pT2a pN0 M0 with clear margins
brief: In a case report published on 4 January 2022, clinicians at St George's Healthcare NHS Trust and East Surrey Hospital in England describe how a smartwatch alert led indirectly to a diagnosis of lung cancer. A previously well 58-year-old man with no significant smoking history received an alert from his smartwatch that his heart rate was irregular and above 180 beats per minute, while he felt nothing.[1] Electrocardiograms in hospital captured no significant arrhythmia, and a cardiologist diagnosed non-sustained ventricular tachycardia from the watch's results. He received an implantable defibrillator. The routine chest X-ray after the procedure happened to show an abnormality in his right upper lung. Further imaging and a biopsy showed an adenocarcinoma, which surgeons removed with clear margins. The cancer lay outside what the watch was built to detect. The authors judge that without the watch the tumor would likely have grown undetected and that curative surgery might not have been an option.[2] The report does not name the watch's brand or model, so its alerting algorithm cannot be identified. It gives no dates for any of the events and no follow-up beyond his discharge on the tenth day after surgery and an outpatient magnetic resonance scan of his heart.

brief: On 20 March 2022 officers of the Hakkari Provincial Police Directorate stopped a car at a checkpoint in Yüksekova, Turkey, after work on the directorate's ASENA analysis program had flagged it. A hidden compartment under the spare-wheel well held 133 packets, 52.5 kg in all, of factory-made explosive assessed as PETN-RDX.[1] The driver was a police officer posted in Istanbul, and on 20 November 2023 the Hakkari 2nd Heavy Penal Court sentenced him to 21 years in prison and four co-defendants to 17.5 years each for supplying weapons to a terrorist organization.[2] ASENA was built to flag drug crime, so this find lay outside its purpose. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu said on 21 March 2022 that police using analysis programs, “what they call artificial intelligence”, had identified a suspicious vehicle thought to be carrying drugs.[3] In June 2022 the head of the police Narcotics Crimes Department listed the explosives among the finds of operations that, by his account, had started with ASENA.[4] No source describes the data that ASENA matched for this car or whether an analyst checked the flag before the stop. The driver spoke in court of “those who informed”, but no source reports an informant.[5]

summary: In a Taiwan trial of 15,965 patients, a neural network flagged high-risk electrocardiograms for physicians, and 90-day mortality was 3.6% versus 4.3% with usual care.
headline: In a Taiwan trial, fewer patients died when AI flagged high-risk ECGs
metric: 3.6% versus 4.3%
brief: A trial in Taiwan tested alerts to physicians from an AI analysis of electrocardiograms, with death from any cause within 90 days as its primary endpoint. At an academic medical center and a community hospital, 15,965 patients were randomly assigned to AI-assisted care or usual care. Ninety-day mortality was 3.6% with AI-assisted care and 4.3% with usual care. The hazard ratio was 0.83, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.70–0.99, so the upper bound lies just below 1, the value of no effect. The research team that developed the system ran the trial.[1] In a paper on randomized trials of cardiovascular AI, researchers at Sheba Medical Center later restated the result without reanalyzing the trial's data, and they judged that mortality gains across these trials were often modest or reached statistical significance mainly in subgroup analyses.[2] The trial measured fewer deaths with the alert pathway. It does not show which clinical actions made the difference. Longer-term survival and whether the result holds in other health systems remain uncertain.

brief: Jessica Cicchino of the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety measured what automatic emergency braking that detects pedestrians does for people on foot in the United States. Using police-reported crashes, she compared vehicles of the same models with and without the optional system. She found that vehicles with the system had a 25% to 27% lower pedestrian crash risk and a 29% to 30% lower pedestrian injury crash risk.[1] She also reported where she found no evidence of benefit: at night on unlit roads, and at speed limits of 50 mph or more. The design is observational, and the abstract names no makers and describes no detection software.[2] Later studies from Japan and from Australia and New Zealand also reported benefits. Automatic emergency braking in some Nissan cars has drawn complaints of false braking that endangered occupants and other road users.

brief: A 78-year-old woman at China Medical University Hospital in Taichung developed severe pneumonia during a prolonged admission. brief: Where breast screening already uses two radiologists, the ScreenTrustCAD study measured what an AI reader adds beside them.[1] At Capio Sankt Göran Hospital in Stockholm, from 1 April 2021 to 9 June 2022, Karolinska Institutet researchers ran Lunit's Insight MMG in the background on the screening mammograms of 55,581 women. brief: A 50-year-old woman who had recently had COVID-19 was referred to the hospital of Oita University in Yufu, Japan, for breathlessness. Four days before admission a primary care physician had measured her oxygen saturation at 94 to 98%, and hospital pulse oximetry read 97%, but her Apple Watch Series 7 had shown 88% in the early morning. In 2023, other authors who examined five studies of the Series 6 with 973 patients found that the watch shows no strong systematic bias against medical-grade pulse oximeters and that outliers of up to 15 points occur.[2] The case depended on clinicians who acted on a watch reading when the hospital reading was normal.[3]

summary: In U.S. police-reported crash data, forward collision warning with automatic emergency braking cut front-to-rear crashes by 49%, and automatic braking cut pickup rear-end crash rates by 43%.
headline: Crash warning and automatic braking cut front-to-rear crashes by 49%
metric: front-to-rear crashes were reduced by 49%
brief: In a final rule of 9 May 2024, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) required automatic emergency braking on new light vehicles in the United States from September 2029. It found that the systems had reduced injuries and saved lives.[1] On 16 November 2022, VOA Learning English reported that PARTS, a partnership of automakers and NHTSA, had found 49% fewer front-to-rear crashes when the striking vehicle had both forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking. It also reported that the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) had found a 43% lower rear-end crash rate for pickups with automatic emergency braking.[2] In the peer-reviewed version of the IIHS study, Jessica Cicchino found in her main analysis that automatic emergency braking was associated with a 34% lower risk of rear-end-striking crashes.[3] In a second study, published on 6 January 2025 and covering model years 2015 to 2023, PARTS again measured a 49% reduction in front-to-rear crashes.[4] The estimates cover the whole system. They do not separate the camera and radar software from the brakes or from the driver who responds to the warning. False positives in Nissan's automatic emergency braking have posed traffic risks to drivers.
system: Forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking across multiple makers' passenger vehicles and pickups
deployer: Multiple automakers (factory-fitted systems)
comparator_against: striking vehicles without forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking
comparator_before: not stated
comparator_after: front to rear crashes were reduced by 49 percent

title: Sepsis alerts from COMPOSER are associated with lower mortality in two emergency departments at UC San Diego Health
summary: After UC San Diego Health deployed COMPOSER, a deep-learning model that alerts nurses to sepsis, mortality was 9.49%, against a modeled 11.39% without it.
headline: Fewer sepsis patients die after COMPOSER alerts UC San Diego nurses
metric: 1.9 percentage points
brief: COMPOSER, a deep-learning model that flags possible sepsis to nurses, went live in two emergency departments at UC San Diego Health on 7 December 2022. The evaluation covered 6,217 adults with sepsis seen before and after that date. Mortality after deployment was 9.49%, against a modeled 11.39% without COMPOSER, an adjusted reduction of 1.9 percentage points with a 95% confidence interval of 0.3–3.5. Raw mortality before deployment was 10.3%. The comparison rests on historical controls, with no randomization and no concurrent untreated group. The estimated benefit reached statistical significance at only one of the two hospitals.[1] A meta-analysis by Yale authors, published on 13 May 2025, pooled seven randomized trials of other sepsis alert systems and found no significant effect on mortality.[2] The COMPOSER team reported in August 2026 that the alerts stayed in use in both emergency departments through October 2025, with a large language model layer added in July 2024. The mortality result is an association, reported by the team that built COMPOSER and the health system that deployed it.

brief: Lund University researchers ran the MASAI trial within the Swedish national screening program. The AI group had 6.4 screen-detected cancers per 1,000 women against 5.0 in the control group, and it needed 44.2% fewer screen readings.[1] The primary outcome, published in The Lancet in 2026, was the interval cancer rate: 1.55 per 1,000 with AI and 1.76 per 1,000 without, which met the trial's non-inferiority margin. title: Kent County Council: Using predictive analytics to prevent homelessness in Maidstone and Kent

headline: Kent reports fewer homeless households after targeted support
brief: Maidstone Borough Council uses an AI-enabled Xantura platform to flag households for proactive homelessness support. In a presentation published on 4 November 2024, a Kent County Council presenter reports that fewer than 1% of flagged households that received support became homeless, against 40% of a group that went without support because the housing team lacked capacity. The groups were not randomized, and the comparison does not separate the effect of the targeting from that of the support. The presenter does not date these outcomes.[1] The UK government's National Plan to End Homelessness, published on 11 December 2025, features Maidstone's use of the platform. Its figures for June 2023 to January 2025 include £440,000 saved in temporary accommodation and 96 homelessness cases avoided, with no stated method.[2] The Centre for Homelessness Impact's randomized trial of similar data-led outreach with Xantura in four other councils was still in progress in June 2026. A family screening tool in a Pennsylvania county also scores households from administrative data, and its scores allegedly fell unevenly on Black families. Kent's presenter states that protected characteristics are not included in the live prediction model.

brief: Operation Renewed Hope ran from 17 July 2023 into early August at the Cyber Crimes Center of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). Mike Prado of HSI said that images enhanced with AI or machine learning can give investigators a starting point.[2] ABC News in Australia reported that Clearview AI's facial recognition was used, and Forbes reported that officials did not confirm Clearview or any specific program.[3] Crikey reported on 25 January 2024 that Australian case material had been analyzed with Clearview AI, which the Australian Federal Police was not allowed to use.[4] The outcomes are ICE's count, and no figure shows how many identifications came from the tools and how many from manual work. In a separate case in Finland, police were reportedly reprimanded after a unit of the National Bureau of Investigation allegedly used Clearview AI to identify potential abuse victims.

summary: Every Cure’s early drug-repurposing system gave high scores to three drugs that a consulting physician had considered for Joseph Coates’s POEMS syndrome; he responded and later reached remission.
headline: A man with a rare blood disorder became well enough for a transplant
metric: he responded within one or two weeks
brief: Public money now goes to the search for new uses of old drugs, and the case of Joseph Coates is told in its support.[1] In January 2024, Coates, 37, of Renton, Washington, was critically ill with POEMS syndrome and too sick for a stem cell transplant. David Fajgenbaum of the University of Pennsylvania and Every Cure recommended three drugs used for multiple myeloma, and Coates’s hematologist and oncologist, Wayne Gao, agreed to give them. Fajgenbaum later explained that an early Every Cure algorithm had also scored those drugs highly.[2] Coates reported that he responded within one or two weeks. He later received a transplant and reported full remission five months after it. Several outlets reported the recovery.[3] In a case series published on 31 May 2023, Mayo Clinic authors reported that five of six patients with relapsed POEMS syndrome responded to regimens built on carfilzomib, one of the three drugs, although none of them received this combination.[4] The part that the algorithm played rests on accounts from Fajgenbaum and Every Cure, because the sources include no detailed case report or case-specific model output and do not establish which algorithm or release scored the drugs.[5]
system: Every Cure’s early drug-repurposing system
developer: Every Cure (co-founded by David Fajgenbaum, University of Pennsylvania)
deployer: David Fajgenbaum (Every Cure / University of Pennsylvania); regimen administered by Wayne Gao, Coates's treating hematologist and oncologist
segment: Individual off-label treatment of a terminal POEMS syndrome patient
comparator_against: the treatments his doctors had tried, with hospice as the remaining option
comparator_before: Coates was now entering a terminal stage: his heart and kidneys were failing, and fluid had to be drained from his belly several times a week. He was too sick to undergo a stem-cell transplant, which could save his life.
comparator_after: within days Coates started to improve. A few months later, he'd recovered sufficiently to receive a stem-cell transplant. He is now in remission.

title: A 76-year-old reads a transient negative T-wave on his own Apple Watch ECG after gym exercise; work-up finds silent three-vessel disease and he has quadruple bypass surgery (Amsterdam UMC)
summary: A 76-year-old saw a transient negative T-wave in a recording from his Apple Watch ECG app after exercise; tests showed three-vessel coronary disease, and he had four bypass grafts.
headline: A 76-year-old spots a change on his Apple Watch ECG and has a bypass
metric: he received four bypass grafts; recovery was uneventful
brief: In a case report published on 30 January 2024, Koster and colleagues at Amsterdam UMC describe a 76-year-old man with no symptoms. On rare occasions and out of interest, he recorded a lead-I electrocardiogram (ECG) on his Apple Watch right after exercise. In the last of these recordings he noticed a negative T-wave that deepened over about seven minutes and returned to normal after 22 minutes. A cardiologist found that his resting ECG and examination were normal, but an exercise test reproduced the change. Imaging then showed three-vessel coronary disease. He received four bypass grafts and recovered uneventfully. The authors report no result from the app's rhythm classifier.[1] The watch recorded the ECG, and the patient read it before his doctors did. Whether he would have come to harm without the recording is not established. The authors write that using the watch to document ischemic changes should be studied systematically before it enters routine clinical care.[2] In a study published on 31 August 2020, cardiologists at Magna Graecia University in Catanzaro moved an Apple Watch around the body to record nine-lead ECGs from 100 participants. They reported that these ECGs agreed with standard 12-lead ECGs in identifying ST-segment changes in patients with heart attacks.[3] This patient recorded lead I alone, so the study bears on his case only in part.
system: Apple Watch ECG app (single lead-I recording; its rhythm classifier is not mentioned in the report)
comparator_against: the cardiologist's resting 12-lead ECG and physical examination
comparator_before: A standard ECG was completely normal, as was physical examination.
comparator_after: he noticed immediately after exercise, a negative T-wave that became more prominent in ∼7 min, then slowly returned back to a normal positive T-wave after 22 min

title: Withings ScanWatch ECG QT measurement leading to congenital long QT syndrome diagnosis and beta-blocker therapy
summary: A Withings ScanWatch displayed a prolonged QT interval that led clinicians in Germany to diagnose inherited long QT syndrome in a father and his daughter and to prescribe nadolol.
headline: Smartwatch readings lead a father and daughter to a long QT diagnosis
metric: displayed values such as QT 506 ms and QTc 457 ms
brief: A man came to the cardiology clinic of University Medical Centre Mannheim, Germany, because of readings from his smartwatch, and the visit led to a diagnosis. The man, an asymptomatic 39-year-old, had recorded single-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) on his Withings ScanWatch out of curiosity, and the watch displayed values such as a QT interval of 506 ms and a corrected QT interval (QTc) of 457 ms. Genetic screening showed a previously unpublished KCNH2 variant, which established congenital long QT syndrome. Nadolol shortened his QTc to 430 ms, and his 7-year-old daughter, who carried the same variant, was also prescribed nadolol.[1] The case report appeared on 4 July 2024 and gives no dates for the events. The diagnosis rested on clinical ECGs and genetic testing, and the report does not say who first noticed the watch's values. Researchers at University Hospital Basel with no tie to Withings tested the ScanWatch's automated QT measurement in 317 patients. They found that the watch measured QTc automatically in 56% of them and concluded that its algorithm needed improvement for clinical use.[2]

title: Smartwatch single-lead ECG captures a 165 bpm wide-complex tachycardia in a 64-year-old man, and Emory cardiologists diagnose ventricular tachycardia and treat it with a defibrillator and an ablation
summary: A smartwatch ECG function of an unnamed brand recorded a 165 bpm wide-complex tachycardia during palpitations, and cardiologists diagnosed ventricular tachycardia and implanted a defibrillator.
headline: Smartwatch ECG captures 165 bpm tachycardia; Emory diagnoses VT
metric: recorded a 165 bpm wide-complex tachycardia during palpitations
brief: In a case report published online on 12 March 2025, authors in the Division of Cardiology at Emory University School of Medicine in Atlanta describe a 64-year-old man with a replaced aortic valve. During palpitations he recorded a single-lead electrocardiogram on his smartwatch, which flagged a heart rate above 150 beats per minute with a warning to speak to a doctor. Clinicians read a wide-complex tachycardia at 165 beats per minute on the trace, and hospital telemetry then recorded episodes of ventricular tachycardia. Doctors implanted a defibrillator, and three months after his discharge it shocked him for ventricular tachycardia. After an ablation, later checks of the device showed no further episodes. The watch did not classify the rhythm, and the authors note that no smartwatch algorithm is validated to detect ventricular tachycardia. The diagnosis came from clinicians. The report does not name the watch's brand or model. The authors write that his ventricular tachycardia would have gone undiagnosed had his clinician not considered the smartwatch data.[1] In a paper published online on 18 November 2025, cardiologists in Haifa with no tie to the Emory team cite the case and pool 20 published patients whose ventricular arrhythmias were captured by smartwatches.[2]

title: Smartwatch “heart arrhythmias” alert leads to a diagnosis of cardiomyopathy caused by premature atrial contractions in a 34-year-old man; ablation lifts his ejection fraction from 15% to 50%
summary: A smartwatch of unstated brand flagged arrhythmias that led to a diagnosis of cardiomyopathy in a 34-year-old man; radiofrequency ablation restored his ejection fraction to 50% at six months.
headline: A smartwatch alert leads a 34-year-old to treatment for a weakened heart
metric: radiofrequency ablation restored his ejection fraction to 50% at six months
brief: In a paper published on 19 December 2025, cardiologists in Thessaloniki note that premature atrial contractions are a major source of false-positive alerts for atrial fibrillation on smartwatches.[1] Here an alert led to the diagnosis of a heart condition that clinicians could treat. A 34-year-old man with no symptoms saw his primary care physician after his smartwatch detected “heart arrhythmias”. An electrocardiogram showed frequent premature atrial contractions, and a cardiologist found an ejection fraction of 35% with a dilated ventricle. Months later, despite heart-failure therapy, imaging showed an ejection fraction of 15%. Radiofrequency ablation stopped the arrhythmia, and at six months he was symptom-free with an ejection fraction of 50%.[2] The watch's part is established only as the trigger. The authors do not identify the device or say what form its alert took, and the rise from 15% to 50% shows the effect of the ablation.[3]
system: Smartwatch arrhythmia detection (brand and model not stated)
developer: Not stated (the report does not name the device's maker)

brief: Columbia University Fertility Center now charges $3,000 for a STAR analysis.[1] The first pregnancy that the center reported with STAR came from a couple who had tried for 19 years to have a child. STAR captured about 2.5 million images of it and detected seven sperm, two of them motile. Embryologists injected the two motile sperm into eggs, and the pregnancy test was positive in March 2025. A girl was born in December 2025. The evidence for the method is one peer-reviewed research letter, written by the team that built STAR, together with figures that the clinic reports about itself.[2] In September 2026 Chia Lin Chang of Chang Gung Memorial Hospital in Taiwan, who declares no conflict of interest, concluded that the case shows that the method is technically feasible. Chang added that the case cannot count as evidence of clinical efficacy without data from a prospective series of cases.[3] Nobody tested whether a longer manual search of the same sample would have found the two sperm, and STAR cannot help men who produce none.[4]

brief: A randomized trial has tested ENAD-DET-01, a polyp-detection system from the South Korean company Ainex. At two Seoul hospitals between May 2023 and April 2025, 998 patients were assigned at random to colonoscopy with or without the system, which draws a circle on the monitor when it detects a polyp. Adenomas were found in 52.3% of patients with the system and 36.1% without.[1] For sessile serrated lesions and cancers, the difference between the groups was not statistically significant. A control rate of 36.1% left room for improvement, and units that already detect more may see a smaller gain. Elsewhere, researchers found no gain in a randomized trial of computer-aided polyp detection at a Japanese community hospital. Both hospitals used one Olympus platform, so the trial does not test the system on other equipment.[2] The Korea Medical Device Development Fund paid for the study, and the authors report no conflicts of interest.

brief: On 10 June 2025, a man suffered a medical episode and sank in the outdoor pool at Stirling Leisure - Inglewood in Perth. Lynxight, a camera system built to detect swimmers in distress, sent lifeguard Cameron Menzies a smartwatch alert with the swimmer's location and images. Another swimmer, Ofer Lefelman, noticed the emergency on his own and lifted the man to the surface.[1] Menzies and fellow lifeguards brought him out of the water. The City of Stirling reports that he was conscious when paramedics took him away and that he later recovered fully.[2] Help came by two routes: The alert reached a lifeguard who had not seen the man sink, and a fellow swimmer noticed him independently.[3] The sources do not show whether he would have survived without the alert.

title: DeepSeek-R1 dialogue leads a 34-year-old man to a genetically confirmed familial Mediterranean fever diagnosis after roughly three decades of symptoms
summary: A patient's dialogue with DeepSeek-R1-0528 pointed to familial Mediterranean fever, genetic testing confirmed it, and colchicine stopped attacks after ~30 years of symptoms.
headline: DeepSeek-R1 flags familial Mediterranean fever, which gene tests confirm
metric: colchicine stopped attacks after ~30 years of symptoms
brief: A 34-year-old man of Egyptian origin had recurrent inflammatory attacks from early childhood, and despite almost three decades of symptoms, extensive investigations had not established a diagnosis. On 28 June 2025 he began a dialogue with the DeepSeek-R1-0528 model, which refined its differential diagnosis toward familial Mediterranean fever and repeatedly advised specialist supervision. He arranged genetic testing himself, and it showed two pathogenic MEFV variants. His attacks stopped on colchicine that he obtained from an Egyptian pharmacy and took on his own, but his liver enzymes rose and the drug was paused.[1] It was resumed at a lower dose under close supervision. In February 2026 he presented to the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf, which confirmed the diagnosis, and he has remained free of attacks.[2] The model's part was the hypothesis and the suggested work-up; the confirmation came from genetic testing and his response to colchicine. The evidence for the benefit comes from one patient. In a study published on 31 October 2025, two rheumatologists in Istanbul found that ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok answered patient questions on familial Mediterranean fever best on recovery and follow-up and less well on diagnosis.[3]
system: DeepSeek-R1
model_version: DeepSeek-R1-0528
segment: Patient-initiated use of a consumer LLM
comparator_against: almost three decades of conventional investigations
comparator_before: Despite almost 3 decades of symptoms, extensive investigations, including contrast-enhanced abdominal CT and MRI, gastroscopy, colonoscopy, and urological assessment, failed to establish a diagnosis.
comparator_after: the diagnosis of FMF was confirmed

title: Federal analysts detect anomalous Medicare billing, and $4.41 billion in claims is held in escrow
summary: Justice Department analysts detected anomalous Medicare billing through proactive data analytics, and $4.41 billion was held in escrow; no source names the software or says that it used AI.
headline: Medicare withholds $4.41 billion in suspected fraudulent payments
metric: held $4.41 billion in escrow from about $4.45 billion scheduled for payment
brief: The Department of Justice reported on 30 June 2025 that its analysts and their partners had detected anomalous Medicare billing in Operation Gold Rush. According to the department, the Office of Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services stopped all but about $41 million of about $4.45 billion scheduled for payment. The $4.41 billion went into escrow, and the Justice Department said that the health agencies intended to seek its return to the Medicare trust fund. Later Justice Department announcements do not say what finally became of that money.[1] Medicare supplemental insurers still paid about $900 million. The Justice Department credits the detection to proactive data analytics, and in the same release it announced plans for an AI-enabled Data Fusion Center. Accountable care organizations had also reported the suspect billing for intermittent urinary catheters, according to the American Hospital Association, and in June 2024 the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services called the 2023 volume of that billing highly suspect.[2] No source shows that AI flagged these claims or says what share of the hold the analytics produced.[3]

brief: A case report published on 12 August 2026 in Resuscitation Plus describes a 69-year-old man who collapsed in ventricular fibrillation while running alone, hidden behind a hedge on a dead-end road.[1] When his Apple Watch detected the fall, it automatically called emergency services on 112 and alerted his emergency contacts. Family members began cardiopulmonary resuscitation about 6–7 minutes after the collapse. An ambulance crew arrived about 1.5 minutes later and defibrillated him, and he made a full neurological recovery. The paper documents that the alerts brought his family to him. It cannot show how long he would have lain there without them, and the comparison rests on an interview in which a son says that he would not otherwise have found his father so quickly.[2] This is a single documented case, echoed by an earlier German report.

brief: In a case report published on 16 January 2026, Hajebian and Friel describe a 22-month-old girl with skull defects that the treating physician did not initially recognize on her computed tomography scan. metric: 36.5% complete skin clearance with zasocitinib versus 13.9% with deucravacitinib at week 16
brief: In the LATITUDE Atlas phase 3 trial, 36.5% of 301 participants on zasocitinib reached complete skin clearance at week 16, against 13.9% of 303 on deucravacitinib. Takeda reports these figures.[1] Takeda also reports that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has granted its application priority review. No approval had been reported by 29 October 2026.[2] In a Cochrane meta-analysis published on 6 August 2025, Sbidian and colleagues included an earlier phase 2b trial of zasocitinib and rated the certainty of evidence as low for most comparisons that involve the drug. They declare no ties to Takeda or Nimbus.[3] The attribution to AI is weaker. Nimbus and Schrödinger developed zasocitinib with computational structure-based design, and Schrödinger describes free-energy calculations and virtual screening. A 2025 Drug Target Review interview with a Takeda scientist describes the approach as AI-assisted.[4] None of these accounts isolates the effect of AI from the rest of the discovery work. Takeda's upfront payment of approximately $4 billion for the program, announced when the acquisition closed in 2023, is no measure of that effect.[5]

brief: In a study published online on 11 June 2026, M. D. Keall of the University of Otago and S. Newstead of the Monash University Accident Research Centre analyzed injury crashes in Australia and New Zealand from 2016 to 2023. Vehicles with pedestrian autonomous emergency braking had a 17% lower rate of pedestrian or cyclist collisions (95% confidence interval 5% to 27%) than vehicles without any autonomous emergency braking (AEB). The rate of collisions with motorcycles was 11% lower with pedestrian AEB, but the lower end of its 95% confidence interval is zero. The design is observational, and the authors relied on vehicle specifications to tell which vehicles had the system.[2]
